top_evidence.document_title: Point-of-care testing for non-communicable diseases and health literacy outcomes: a systematic review
top_evidence.text: This study was strengthened by the rigorous systematic review process conducted in line with the PRISMA statement [17]. Eligibility criteria were explicitly defined prior to commencing the literature search, with no restrictions imposed on language, region, or study type. The search strategy was methodologically developed in collaboration with an experienced research librarian, following multiple pilot searches to refine database queries and MeSH terms across several databases to maximise coverage. Although comprehensive, the omission of device-specific and risk-factor terms may have limited retrieval of eligible studies, and citation searching was not undertaken. Future reviews should expand search terms to include specific NCDs, risk factors, and device-specific terminology to ensure broader coverage. Study screening and data extraction were independently undertaken by two researchers, achieving high agreement, which improves reliability compared to single screening methods [35]. Included studies were limited to publications from the five years prior to the search, an intentional scope decision aligned with WHO guidance to capture contemporary evidence for POC tests and health literacy definitions. As the final search was conducted in May 2023, the study is limited in its consideration of more recent evidence or developments in POC testing, and the findings should be interpreted as reflecting the evidence base up to that date. Although newer studies may now exist, findings remain highly relevant and provide a valuable foundation for understanding the role of modern POC testing in health literacy. Additionally, 11 full-text reports were unable to be retrieved, largely due to being abstract-only or presented in nonwritten formats. While these reports may lack sufficient methodological detail for full appraisal, their exclusion may still introduce retrieval bias and contribute to the narrow evidence base identified. Meta-analysis was not feasible due to variability between interventions, disease focus, measurement tools, and population characteristics. Outcomes were assessed using diverse instruments, ranging from validated tools (e.g. PAM-13) to study-developed questionnaires, qualitative interviews, and clinical markers of adherence or control. This mix of validated and self-reported proxy measures introduces differences in measurement rigour, further limiting comparability across studies. Despite this, shared self-reported proxy outcomes such as patient knowledge, confidence, engagement, and behaviour change enabled narrative synthesis via the framework of WHO health literacy actions. Designs were predominantly cross-sectional or short-term, with limited longitudinal follow-up. Furthermore, equity indicators were inconsistently reported, limiting disaggregated analysis. Although age and sex variables were consistently reported, ethnicity and socioeconomic indicators were often absent, restricting the ability to generalise findings to diverse populations. These limitations highlight the need for more consistent measurements using validated health literacy instruments, longer follow-ups, and systematic equity reporting in future work. While risk of bias assessment using the MMAT demonstrated generally strong methodological quality across the included studies, several limitations were also identified. Several studies did not adequately account for potential confounders, making it difficult to isolate the contribution of POC testing. Two studies did not meet the criterion for appropriate interpretation of results based on the data provided [27, 29], however this was addressed by considering only the raw outcome data in the synthesis. One study did not meet the criterion for low non-response bias [30], potentially affecting the representativeness of its findings. Although these issues were present in a minority of studies, they may reduce confidence in some reported associations and should be considered when interpreting the overall strength of the evidence base.

top_evidence.text: The review protocol was registered with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; registration number CRD42022348011). A full protocol may be requested from the authors. Amendments to the original protocol included changes in author contributions, and health literacy outcomes were synthesised according to the World Health Organization (WHO) health literacy domains. The review was conducted and reported in line with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Additional file 1) [17].

top_evidence.document_title: Point-of-care testing for non-communicable diseases and health literacy outcomes: a systematic review
top_evidence.text: Background Health literacy responsiveness has been identified as a key action area in reducing the burden of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), which are a leading cause of death worldwide. Point-of-care (POC) testing has the potential to improve health literacy in individuals and communities. This systematic review aimed to synthesise the literature regarding POC testing for NCDs and health literacy outcomes. Methods A systematic search was conducted across seven databases, Medline (via OVID), PsycINFO, Emcare, Scopus, ProQuest (Health databases), CINAHL, and Web of Science, between May 2018 and May 2023. Studies that investigated the utilisation of a POC device for measurement of NCD markers, and reported at least one outcome measure of health literacy in individuals over 10 years old were eligible for inclusion. Risk of bias in included studies was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Results were mapped to the five WHO health literacy actions through narrative synthesis. Results Thirteen studies were eligible for inclusion, primarily investigating POC assessment of diabetes, with some examining lipids or coagulation. Study cohorts were geographically limited to eight countries in predominantly high-income settings. Following POC testing relevant to diabetes and cardiovascular contexts, patients reported an enhanced understanding of health, motivation to make positive lifestyle changes, increased quality of life and decreased worry, increased confidence, and improved health markers. Conclusion The findings from this review suggest that POC testing may support improvements in individual health literacy outcomes relevant to NCD management, specifically in diabetes and cardiovascular contexts. These findings reflect the potential of POC testing to contribute to more responsive health systems, by improving accessibility, results delivery, and communication of health information. However, the evidence base is limited in scope, and findings may not necessarily be generalisable. Future studies should prioritise examining a broader range of NCDs, particularly in underdeveloped regions, and employ specific validated health literacy tools. Prospero registration CRD42022348011. top_evidence.text: Resulting records from each database were imported into EndNote 20 where duplicates were provisionally removed. Records were then uploaded to Covidence systematic review management software [18] where a final duplication detection test was conducted. Titles and abstracts of resulting records were initially screened against eligibility criteria by two researchers (KM and LD), independently. Agreement between reviewers was high at 96.7%, with consensus required for further screening. Remaining records underwent independent full-text screening by the same two researchers (KM and LD), with consensus required for inclusion in the review. Agreement at full-text screening was 85.7%, with discrepancies resolved through discussion or, if necessary, adjudication by a third reviewer (MS).

top_evidence.section: Risk Of Bias In Individual Studies
top_evidence.text: Risk of bias (quality) of individual studies was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) [19]. The MMAT assessed included studies based on the study design; qualitative only, quantitative (non-randomised, randomised, descriptive), or mixed methods. Risk of bias was assessed by two independent researchers, with any discrepancies resolved through discussion or a third reviewer. Studies were not allocated a rating based on recommendations from the MMAT author [19].

top_evidence.document_title: Point-of-care testing for non-communicable diseases and health literacy outcomes: a systematic review
top_evidence.text: Eight studies met al.l quality criteria assessed by the MMAT [20-26, 28]. The MMAT assessment showed consistently clear research questions and appropriate data collection across most studies. However, two quantitative studies did not meet criteria for the interpretation of results based on the data provided [27, 29], while two did not account for confounders in analyses [31, 32]. One descriptive study failed to meet the criteria of low nonresponse bias [30]. All results from the risk of bias assessment can be seen in Additional file 3.

top_evidence.document_title: Point-of-care testing for non-communicable diseases and health literacy outcomes: a systematic review
top_evidence.text: To our knowledge, this study is among the first to systematically review the literature on pathology-based POC testing for NCDs focusing on health literacy outcomes. Following systematic searches, thirteen studies conducted across eight countries were identified, investigating POC testing for diabetes/glucose, lipids, or coagulation management. POC testing is not yet widely available for the direct assessment of cancer or mental health conditions, and no eligible studies were identified for chronic respiratory diseases. As such, the evidence base is restricted to diabetes and cardiovascular contexts, with most studies focused on diabetes. Included studies employed diverse methodologies (quantitative, qualitative, and mixed methods), but findings were generally consistent despite heterogeneity. Evidence suggested that access to POC testing may be associated with improvements across the WHO's five actions of health literacy: Access , Understand , Appraise , Remember , and Use health information. Qualitative interviews consistently identified that access to health information was perceived as enhanced through the immediacy of POC test results [20-24]. Rapid feedback of results was reported to reduce delays and uncertainty, creating opportunities for patients to engage and communicate with clinicians more effectively [20, 24]. This was a consistent theme for parents of children with diabetes, who reported increased confidence in managing their child's condition [21, 22]. These findings suggest that the rapid nature of POC testing may be associated with supporting health literacy, not only by improving direct access to health information, but also by fostering more meaningful interactions between patients and health professionals. Patients and parents using POC technologies for diabetes monitoring also reported enhanced understanding of their own [23, 24] or their child's [21, 22] health, including greater awareness of how lifestyle habits (e.g. diet) influenced outcomes [22-24], and improved comprehension of test results and clinical thresholds [20, 23]. These insights were complemented by quantitative proxy measures, including improvements in PAM13 scores [25, 28], self-rated knowledge scores [32], and Likert scale assessments of understanding [30] and empowerment [29]. While PAM-13 is not a direct measure of health literacy, it is a validated tool that assesses an individual's knowledge, skills, and confidence in managing their health [12], aligning with WHO's actions of appraising , understanding , and using health information. Together, these findings suggest that POC testing may be associated with improved clinical understanding and reinforcement of the connection between health and lifestyle behaviours. Appraising health information involves evaluating its relevance and implications for management [8], which was reflected through reports of reduced uncertainty and increased confidence in managing health. In qualitative studies, participants reported that POC testing for diabetes and coagulation reduced worry and improved quality of life [21, 22, 24, 29], while others described increased satisfaction, empowerment, and confidence in managing their health [23, 24, 27]. These findings were supported by quantitative improvements in PAM-13 scores [25, 28], and higher satisfaction and quality of life ratings [31]. In qualitative interviews, diabetes patients reported remembering and clarifying health information at the time of consultation when POC testing was used [20, 23]. POC testing in diabetes contexts was also associated with more consistent medication adherence [23]. These observations were reinforced by findings in coagulation monitoring, where associations with improved adherence was reflected in increased proportion of days covered (PDC) [26] and INR control [31, 32]. These results suggest that POC testing interventions may assist recall of health requirements, supported by measurable associations with improvements in treatment adherence. The ability to access , understand , appraise , and remember health information appeared to be associated with the translation of knowledge into action through use. Across studies, participants reported adoption of positive lifestyle behaviours, such as dietary changes and increased physical activity [21-24, 30]. Quantitative data showed associations with improvements in medication adherence [26, 31, 32], and reductions in high HbA1c levels (> 9%) [25, 28]. Even a 1% decrease in HbA1c is associated with a significant reduction in diabetes-related complications, including cardiovascular disease, kidney damage, nerve damage, and eye problems [33, 34]. Collectively, these findings indicate that POC testing interventions may facilitate the translation of health information into action, supporting lifestyle change and improved disease management. It is important to note that POC testing is rarely delivered in isolation, with communication of results also strongly influencing patient understanding and engagement. Mechanisms such as the immediacy of results, personalised provider explanation, and access to additional resources may reinforce knowledge, confidence, and comfort. Visible biomarker changes may strengthen the perceived link between behaviour and health outcomes, while integration into routine care can help normalise engagement and build confidence. In practice, POC testing was commonly delivered alongside broader care such as health consultations, community health events, and additional health measurements (e.g. blood pressure). These multi-layered interventions introduce several factors that may shape health knowledge and behaviour, and therefore, the observed outcomes cannot be attributed to POC testing alone. Rather, the findings highlight how POC testing, when combined with responsive communication and supportive care processes, may contribute to health literacy outcomes.
